new_statements.quote: 2. Tone and Stress 2a. Tone The importance of Tone has not yet been fully investigated. A few lexical Tone doublets have been recorded, e.g.: LARO (K-M) 'yoré axes; 'yore fences MASAKIN ti thorn; ti fire; di egg; di thigh 2b. Stress According to Stevenson 'dynamic Stress, accompanied by High or Low tone, plays a greater role than syllabic pitch as such, but is not equally prominent in all languages'. Examples are not marked for tone or stress. 3. Word Shape The simplest form of the word is monosyllabic or disyllabic, VCV being common. In T-M Noun Stems often consist of VCV, Verb Stems of CVC.

new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (no catalog record, no existing statement for Tocho). The statement applies to Tocho only through its membership of the Talodi(-Masakin) group; it gives stress type (dynamic, with H/L tone) but no placement, so it is not a catalog-ready placement rule. Consistent with the on-file OPSL sources (Spronk 2004, Norton & Alaki 2015), which report two tone levels and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement for the Koalib-Moro / Talodi-Masakin / Lafofa 'class languages' as a whole, quoted from Stevenson: word stress exists and is 'dynamic' (intensity-based), co-occurs with High or Low tone and outweighs syllabic pitch, but is 'not equally prominent in all languages' of the group; no position of stress is stated, no Tocho (Tacho) data are given (the Talodi-Masakin data are labelled MASAKIN, TALODI and ELIRI; Tacho/Tocho/Lumun/Jomang do not occur in the volume's indexed text), and 'Examples are not marked for tone or stress'. Tone: 'importance.. not yet fully investigated', a few lexical tone doublets (Laro, Masakin). So: stress asserted, placement unstated -> not a placement rule for Tocho.
new_statements.exceptions: only that stress 'is not equally prominent in all languages' of the group; examples unmarked for tone or stress
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan 1966 ch. 18a treats the 'class languages' Koalib-Moro, Talodi-Masakin and Lafofa at group level; its Talodi-Masakin data are labelled MASAKIN, TALODI and ELIRI, and Tacho/Tocho (taz) is never named in the volume (it is listed with Torona and Lumun in the Talodi cluster of the Moro Hills in the authors' 1956 handbook). The stress remark therefore bears on Tocho only by group membership, not as a description of the Tocho variety.

tone_statements.citation: Norton, Russell. 2018. Parallel grammar documentation in four Talodi languages. Afrikanistik-Aegyptologie-Online (AAeO) 2018: 1-34. Cologne: Institut fuer Afrikanistik und Aegyptologie, Universitaet zu Koeln. doi:10.18716/ojs/aaeo/2018_3457; urn:nbn:de:0009-10-48877.
tone_statements.quote: Tone presents a more serious problem: since tone is not marked in the orthographies of the languages in this survey, tone is also absent from the phonetic re-transcriptions of the writers’ data in this survey. Talodi languages appear to fit a type of [...] African language in which tone has a low functional load in the lexicon [...] No grammatical category surveyed here was found to be marked by a minimal tone contrast on written homographs in all four languages. However, tone is known to have a role in forming imperative verbs in both Lumun and Dagik [...] imperative tone goes back to proto-Talodi and is therefore likely to be inherited by further Talodi languages.
